After informing the airport authorities, one inspector, accompanied by seven personnel, including three women police officers, entered the aircraft and asked the trio to disembark. clusters.text: Apple is preparing new displays and large numbers of demo units for the iPhone Duo 's October 23 launch, but supply will be limited, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman . Ahead of the October 23 launch, Apple plans to set aside a section of its Fifth Avenue flagship store for the ‌iPhone Duo‌. Most locations will add an extra spotlight table for the device, using Apple's white display tables with central posts. Gurman said a new fixture will show how the phone folds and unfolds. The number of demonstration devices will vary considerably between locations. Fifth Avenue in New York is expected to receive more than 150 units for customers to try and for other displays, compared with nearly 100 at the Apple Park Visitor Center. Non-flagship stores will receive approximately 20 units each on average. Three other prominent stores will fall between those allocations: Chicago's Michigan Avenue, The Grove in Los Angeles, and Manhattan's Upper West Side. Each is expected to have approximately 30 to 40 devices. Visitors will be able to explore StandBy on untethered phones in the Avenue display areas along the sides of stores. For comparisons on store tables, Apple has designed a MagSafe stand that accommodates an open ‌iPhone Duo‌ and two conventional iPhones. The retail preparations come as Apple faces tighter supply than it had anticipated. According to Gurman, around two months ago the company believed production constraints could prevent sales from starting until later in November. It has since assembled sufficient inventory to proceed with this month's release, although stock is expected to remain limited. But he said AI is more dangerous than cars, planes or medicines, all of which are heavily regulated, and that "there are some grim possibilities if we don't maintain control."Bill Gates says a middle ground on AI regulation existsGates said the AI industry is doing its job by raising the alarm. What isn't getting across, he argued, is that the risks can be kept down "if we're judicious". He blamed part of that on governments that swing between two extremes: "let's not have any safeguards" or "let's completely stop this".The world found a workable balance for planes, cars and drugs, he said, and AI needs the same. Finding that balance is something "we don't have a lot of sophistication" in right now, he added, "but I do believe that middle ground exists." clusters.text: Monthly investments through systematic investment plans (SIPs) in mutual funds touched a record ₹ 32,490 crore in September 2026, up from ₹ 32,297 crore in August, according to data released by the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI). The equity mutual funds also attracted stronger inflows during the month, even as the mutual fund industry recorded an overall net outflow, largely due to the substantial withdrawals from different fixed-income schemes. Net inflows into equity mutual funds rose to ₹ 38,307 crore in September from ₹ 29,328 crore in August, an increase of around 30.6% month-on-month. The small-cap mutual funds attracted ₹ 9,039 crore, in comparison with ₹ 7,973 crore in August. Mid-cap fund inflows rose to ₹ 7,835 crore from ₹ 6,989 crore, while flexi-cap schemes added inflows of ₹ 6,702 crore, up from ₹ 5,059 crore. The sectoral thematic funds saw inflows increase to ₹ 3,640 crore from ₹ 1,713 crore. Large-cap mutual funds also returned to positive territory, attracting ₹ 859 crore after net outflows of ₹ 1,147 crore in August. These figures highlight stronger investment flows into equity schemes, although monthly inflows alone are not an indication of future market performance. Even after record SIP contributions and very strong equity inflows, the mutual fund industry recorded net outflows of ₹ 1.33 lakh crore in September, compared with ₹ 41,353 crore in August. Fixed-income mutual funds accounted for the majority of the pressure, recording net outflows of ₹ 1.83 lakh crore in September, against ₹ 8,127 crore in August. The industry's net asset under management (AUM) declined to ₹ 82.64 lakh crore in September from ₹ 87.08 lakh crore in August. The record SIP figures underscore continued investor enthusiasm and participation in equity markets. However, investors should ensure they choose mutual fund schemes aligned with their long-term economic objectives, investment horizon and risk tolerance, rather than relying solely on monthly inflow trends. clusters.text: This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: An international team of researchers has uncovered new evidence illuminating the evolutionary origins of one of the defining features of mammals: the ability to suckle and consume milk during infancy. Their findings, published in Nature , suggest that key anatomical structures required for mammalian suckling, swallowing and breastfeeding behaviors evolved nearly 165 million years ago, long before the appearance of modern mammals. The findings describe a newly discovered species called Megacauda sungei, a large mammaliaform that lived during the Middle Jurassic Period in what is now Inner Mongolia, China. The research was led by scientists from the University of Chicago, Shenyang Normal University, Shandong University of Science and Technology, the University of Bonn and Ohio University. Using high-resolution microCT imaging, the team reconstructed the skull and skeletal anatomy of the fossil. They discovered an unexpected combination of traits. Megacauda had specialized blade-like cheek teeth resembling those of modern seals, a platypus-like pelvis and an otter-like tail, indicating it was likely a semiaquatic predator that hunted small vertebrates and invertebrates in freshwater environments. More significantly, the researchers identified a pair of small bony projections on the roof of the mouth that closely resemble features found in living therian mammals, a group that includes marsupials (such as kangaroos and opossums) and placental mammals (such as elephants and humans). In modern mammals, these structures help support the soft palate and muscles involved in suckling, swallowing and protecting the airway. Because soft tissues are rarely preserved in fossils, scientists have long struggled to determine when these important feeding structures first evolved. "The anatomy of Megacauda suggests that structures involved in coordinating swallowing and sucking had already begun to evolve by the Middle Jurassic. This discovery helps us better understand the biological foundations of one of the defining characteristics of mammals: feeding young with milk," said Zhe-Xi Luo, Ph.D., professor of organismal biology and anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of the study. clusters.text: Cole Palmer missed the 2026 World Cup after struggling last season with chronic injury The Premier League may have just returned from a three-week break, but for many of its stars there was no rest at all. Of all the Premier League players called up by their countries, 25 played 360 minutes - the full length of four games - during the extended international break. These included 13 players who featured for their clubs at the World Cup, such as Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk, who also played 55 games for his club last season. Van Dijk is one of several players, including England's Declan Rice, Morgan Rogers and Harry Kane, who played more than 4,000 minutes in all competitions in 2025-26 and have started on a similar trajectory this season. According to expert sports scientists and psychologists, this cannot be maintained. "It is not sustainable," Dr Dave Richardson, head of psychology, sports science and wellbeing at the University of Lincoln, told BBC Sport. "We will start to see more clamour when we are not happy with the quality of performances; the public pay to see high quality." Vince told BBC Radio Gloucestershire that he initially refused Peterborough permission to speak to Savage. He said he was forced to agree to the move after the League One side approached his former manager directly before appointing him on 2 October. "He's [Savage] a friend and it was very hard to say no, so I said 'fine, go and talk to them'," said Vince. "Peterborough themselves have covered themselves in no glory here. They came to us and said 'we would like to speak to your manager'. "We said no and so they spoke to him and then he came to us and said 'I hear Peterborough want to speak to me'. So, that's an illegal approach." However, Posh chairman MacAnthony, writing on X, said the process to appoint a new manager was "100% correct and proper, following all the rules". Late last month, National League side Forest Green announced that Savage, 51, had been given permission to speak to another club, before confirming he had been offered the Peterborough job, following the departure of Luke Williams. "In the negotiations, Peterborough paid no respect to Robbie's position," said Vince. "He was stuck in the middle. He went there on the Monday, they offered him the job verbally and then they denied offering him the job. "Then they said they were going to move on to their second choice, leaving him in a real pickle, and we had no choice but to say 'look, just take him, that's the best thing for him'." Vince added: "Robbie is a friend and told us he had an intense personal need to leave. It was impossible to have a proper negotiation. "In the end, we said 'look, just take him on your terms'. We cared more about Robbie than the outcome. "Football is not a bad place, but there's people in it that give it a bad name. Enough said." In response, MacAnthony added: "I have been an owner for 20 years in the EFL and have respect for the process. Forest Green have not confirmed if they have contacted the Football Association about the matter. Learn More India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has become the backbone of everyday digital payments, from paying for groceries to settling large bills. As the system prepares for a merchant charge on higher-value transactions, a new report has argued that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) framework needs rationalisation to protect public trust in UPI. The report, written by an academic and a former central bank official, suggests a much lower charge, a different way of sharing it between participants and a greater role for banks in funding UPI's upkeep. The merchant discount rate is the fee a merchant pays to the payments ecosystem for accepting a digital payment. For several years, UPI payments to merchants have largely been free of such charges, which helped drive rapid adoption across shops, small businesses and online platforms. On September 15, the UPI Steering Committee set an MDR of 0.40 per cent on person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions above Rs 2,000. The framework is scheduled to take effect from October 15, 2026. Trade bodies have asked the government to roll back the charge, arguing that it could burden merchants who have embraced UPI. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra, for his part, has said that a small MDR is unlikely to hurt UPI volumes. The report enters this debate with a set of alternative proposals.
